evidence: Ter. Ph. 575: senectūs ipsa est morbus
terms.comment: To fall ill: in morbum incidere, morbō corripī (see ill); to catch a disease, morbum contrahere (M-O s.v. catch (a disease), from Pliny). An attack of illness: impetus or accessiō (Traupman 62).

evidence: Cic. Tusc. 4.29: morbum appellant tōtīus corporis corruptiōnem, aegrōtātiōnem morbum cum imbēcillitāte (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Lewis & Short: properly only of the body, and much used in Cicero’s philosophical works; aegritūdō is classically grief.
Any evil or misfortune, and so a complaint of the body; plural mala, ills.

phrases.english: Old age is itself a disease.

phrases.latin: opprime, dum nova sunt, subitī mala sēmina morbī
phrases.english: crush the evil seeds of a sudden disease while they are new

phrases.latin: ego autem quom omnīs morbōs reformīdō …
phrases.english: but I, since I dread every disease …
